intro: This is a 55-minute conversation with one interviewer, one of the rounds in the onsite loop. Nothing is submitted beforehand. What you bring is a specific, considered answer to why you want to work at Anthropic and on AI safety, a decision process that holds up as a hypothetical dilemma is pushed further with follow-up questions, a defensible opinion — including real disagreement — on the company's own published safety commitments, a set of personal stories with concrete stakes, and a separate read on your character and judgment, including one prompt argued live in the room. The questions fall into five groups.
solutionIntro: The round can run as a direct sequence of the questions above, or as an open-ended conversation that never names AI safety at all; either way, the same five groups are what gets assessed, so prepare the same material regardless of how the conversation opens. Pace yourself inside the 55 minutes: aim for two to three minutes per story, with a clear arc from the situation to your action to what you took from it, and let a follow-up draw out more rather than front-loading every detail.

groups.title: Motivation and mission
groups.guidance:
What it probes: whether your answer to "why Anthropic" and "why AI safety" is backed by something specific to you — a value you can name and a piece of your own history that actually supports it — rather than a sentence that would work at any AI company, and whether "what could Anthropic do better" gets a real, considered answer instead of a complaint or agreement with everything.

Skeleton: name one specific value Anthropic states for itself, say concretely why you hold that value independent of Anthropic — you should be able to name when you first noticed you cared about it — give one example from your own life or work, from before you considered working there, where you acted on it, and connect it to a specific, verifiable piece of your work history: a project, a decision, or the field you moved into and why. Treat "what would make you leave" and "what could Anthropic do better" as calibration checks rather than loyalty tests: name one real condition under which you would leave — a change in the work itself, not a vague "if things got bad" — and one specific, defensible tension you see in how the company operates, for example between how fast it ships and how much safety evaluation that pace leaves room for, stated as a tradeoff rather than a grievance.

Most common way to lose points: an answer general enough to fit any AI lab ("the mission is important", "AGI is exciting"), a value cited with no example of living it, or a "what could Anthropic do better" that is either agreement dressed up as an answer or ordinary product feedback with no connection to values, safety, or how the company operates. Fix: before the round, write down the one value and the one piece of personal evidence for it, and one specific, real critique stated as what it costs to fix rather than as a complaint.

questions.q: Why Anthropic, specifically — as opposed to another lab or company working on related problems?
Which one of Anthropic's stated values resonates with you personally, and why — with a concrete example of when you acted on it, not merely admired it?
Why does AI safety matter to you personally, rather than as a cause that would fit any AI employer?
How does your past work — the specific projects, decisions, or field you came from — actually connect to that concern?
What would make you want to leave Anthropic?
What could Anthropic do better?

groups.title: Hypothetical dilemmas
groups.guidance:
What it probes: whether your reasoning stays consistent as each follow-up changes one fact. There is no single correct verdict on whether to delay; what is being assessed is a decision process you can name and keep applying as the scenario is pushed further.

Skeleton: answer the opening risk question in two or three sentences — one mechanism you actually take most seriously, one observation that would change your view. Then, before the first version of the breakthrough scenario, state your actual decision criteria — for example, how reversible the potential harm is, how quickly it would become visible, and whether a narrower release could capture some of the benefit while more evidence is gathered — rather than jumping straight to "delay" or "ship." For each follow-up, name explicitly which fact changed and how it moves you against those same criteria, instead of picking a new answer from scratch:

  • If you support slowing down broadly: separate whether slowing down is the right call from whether it changes what a competitor does. A safety practice you would take unilaterally does not stop being correct just because it fails to change the outcome industry-wide; say so, and name what you would actually do to make it count beyond your own team, such as pushing for external commitments or shared evaluation work.
  • If a competitor does not slow down: say plainly that this does not by itself change whether the original action was right, but that it does change which options are open to you — from unilateral caution toward advocating for coordination you do not control alone.
  • If that leaves you or your team visibly behind: distinguish behind on a competitive metric from ceding the field to less careful actors, name which one you are actually worried about, and what you would do about it operationally, in your own words, rather than an abstract "we would catch up."
  • For the commercial-deadline-versus-safety version: ask what you would need to know first — what the actual risk is, what is really driving the deadline, and whether it can move or the release can be narrowed — then propose an option that serves both constraints, worked out with whoever owns the safety or privacy review rather than decided by you alone. If you are still asked to cross a line you consider real, escalate through a named channel, tell whoever asked that you are doing so, and leave a written record of the risk, the alternative you proposed, and who signed off on proceeding anyway.
  • For the equity-to-zero version: separate what you can actually assess right now — the effect on your current work and any near-term operational risk — from what you cannot yet know, communicate early and honestly with your manager rather than deciding alone, and be honest that your own tolerance for the risk is a legitimate part of your answer rather than performing indifference to it.

Most common way to lose points: giving a single fixed verdict ("I would always delay" or "I would never delay") and defending it unchanged through every follow-up, or flipping your answer at each follow-up without saying which fact moved you — both read as reasoning that is not actually connected to the criteria you started with. Fix: write out, for at least the breakthrough scenario, the two or three criteria you would actually use and the fact that would flip your decision, so that each follow-up in the round becomes "that changes criterion X, so here is how my answer moves" rather than a new answer picked from scratch.

questions.q: Which risk from more capable AI do you personally take most seriously, and what evidence would change your view of it?
Your team produces a genuine capability breakthrough, but its risk is not yet well understood or quantified. Would you delay releasing it for safety reasons, and on what basis?
Do you support slowing down AI progress broadly for safety, even where the decision is not solely yours to make?
What do you do if you hold back and a competing lab does not?
What do you do if that choice leaves you, or your team, visibly behind?
Separately: you are caught between a commercial deadline and a safety, reliability, or privacy concern you believe is real. How do you decide what to do?
If Anthropic's equity value fell to zero, or the company faced a severe operating or financial crisis, how would you respond — in your own work, and in how you communicate with your manager and team?

groups.title: Critical engagement with Anthropic's public commitments
groups.guidance:
What it probes: whether you have actually read the company's own public commitments and can hold a specific, defensible opinion about them — including a real disagreement — rather than reciting them back approvingly or rejecting them without being able to describe them accurately.

Skeleton: name the specific commitment you are discussing precisely enough that the interviewer can tell you have read it, not a secondhand summary; state one part you agree with and the real tradeoff it makes, not just that it "makes sense"; state one part you would change, and be precise about what that change would cost, since loosening a commitment buys speed at the cost of risk and tightening one buys safety margin at the cost of falling behind on deployment; and close by naming where you are genuinely unsure rather than asserting a confidence you do not have.

Most common way to lose points: two opposite failures — agreeing with everything, which reads as not having engaged with the material, and disagreeing with something you cannot describe accurately, which reads as posturing. Fix: read the documents themselves rather than relying on secondhand summaries, and walk in with one specific point of agreement and one specific point of disagreement, each tied to a real tradeoff rather than an up-or-down verdict. Worth having actually read before the round:

  • Core Views on AI Safety — Anthropic's own public explanation of its overall reasoning about AI risk and why it works on frontier AI at all.
  • The Responsible Scaling Policy — Anthropic's public policy tying how capable a model is allowed to become to the safety and security work required alongside it.
  • Claude's Constitution — Anthropic's public document on the values and character it aims to train into Claude.
  • The Long-Term Benefit Trust — Anthropic's public description of the governance body meant to represent its mission independent of shareholder interest.

questions.q: Anthropic publishes its own safety commitments, including a scaling policy that sets out when it will restrict or pause deploying a model that has become more capable. Which specific part of a commitment like that do you agree with, and why?
Which specific part would you change — tighten, loosen, or argue against entirely — and what would that change trade away?
Have you engaged with Anthropic's own public reasoning about AI safety and its approach to training a model's values? What do you actually think of it?

groups.title: Values stories
groups.guidance:
What it probes: personal evidence for eight distinct claims — persuadable; able to repair a relationship, not just avoid or win it; will hold a safety, reliability, or privacy concern under real pressure to drop it; can disagree with authority and say how; can admit fault rather than reframe it; can reason a moral conflict through to a decision, not just call it hard; keeps revising judgment of past conduct rather than fixing it where you first landed; will pay a real cost to keep a value nothing forced you to. Eight different stories are needed, each with its own action and a verifiable result.

Skeleton: situation, your position at the time, the new information or argument that entered, what you did in response, the result, and what you do differently now. For the persuaded story, name the actual evidence that moved you, not seniority or insistence, and what you did afterward to act on it. For the relationship-repair story, state your own share of the breakdown and the concrete action that rebuilt trust, not "we talked it out." For the moral-dilemma story, name the two things in tension and what you knowingly gave up. For the now-consider-wrong story, say what let you go through with it then and what has actually changed since — new information, a changed standard, plain hindsight. For the pressure story, name the real cost of holding the value: one that cost nothing proves nothing.

Most common way to lose points: reusing one all-purpose conflict story across several prompts, offering a technical or scheduling disagreement for a question about a value, or collapsing the moral-dilemma, admitted-mistake, and now-consider-wrong prompts into one story because all three involve being at fault. Fix: map eight stories one-to-one to the prompts — a dilemma is a choice between two legitimate claims, a mistake is an error you owned and corrected, something you now consider wrong is a verdict that arrived later — and keep at least one conflict story turning on a principle, not a scheduling preference.

Story The failure mode specific to it
Persuaded and changed your mind Credits the other person's seniority or persistence instead of the actual evidence that moved you
Repaired a damaged relationship Describes the fix as one conversation, with no concrete action that rebuilt trust over time
Safety/reliability/privacy concern that slowed a launch No real evidence for the risk, or no honest account of what raising it cost you
Disagreed with leadership Vague about how the disagreement was actually raised, or silent on the real outcome
Admitted a mistake Reframes the mistake as someone else's fault or as a miscommunication rather than a wrong call
Faced a moral dilemma Calls the choice hard without naming the two competing claims
Something you now consider wrong Re-justifies the original call rather than revising it
Upheld a value under pressure Picks a value that cost nothing, under no real pressure

questions.q: Tell me about a time someone persuaded you to change a position you had genuinely held and argued for — what changed your mind?
Tell me about a working relationship that broke down, and how you repaired it.
Tell me about a time you raised a safety, reliability, or privacy concern that slowed down or blocked a launch.
Tell me about a time you disagreed with a decision made by someone with authority over you, and pushed back on it.
Tell me about a mistake you made where you were the one who was wrong, and how you handled it.
Tell me about a moral dilemma you actually faced — two obligations pulling in different directions — and how you decided between them.
Tell me about something you did that you now judge to have been wrong, though it did not feel that way then, and how you have reconciled it since.
Tell me about a time you held to a value under real, uncomfortable pressure to abandon it.

groups.title: Character and judgment
groups.guidance:
What it probes: what has shaped you outside a single decision, whether an interest survives with no payoff, whether you can argue live under real pushback, and how you handle scale and ambiguity with no single right move.

Skeleton: for the transformative-experience prompt, name the before-and-after — a belief, habit, or priority different now — not a dramatic event; a personal example counts as much as a work one. For the no-payoff prompt, name the thing precisely and what keeps you doing it unwatched. For the disliked-task prompt, name it honestly, then, once the interviewer claims the same dislike, change the arrangement of the work rather than only argue for it — a shared rotation, automation, or making the task's value visible to whoever does not see it — and only briefly say why it still has to happen. For the complex-situation prompt, name the actual sources of complexity — independent moving parts, misaligned incentives, the uncertainty you acted under — and what made it yours to resolve.

Most common way to lose points: an event with no stated change in belief or behavior; a no-payoff answer that is quietly instrumental; a disliked-task answer repeating the argument that already failed in the prompt itself; a complex-situation answer long to narrate but not actually hard to resolve. Fix: for the disliked-task prompt, prepare a structural change — a rotation, automation, or a way of surfacing the task's value — rather than a better argument, since repeating a failed argument is the failure itself.

questions.q: What has been the most personally transformative experience of your life, inside work or outside it, and what changed in how you operate afterward?
Tell me about something you keep doing purely because you care about it, with no practical payoff.
Name the task you enjoy least — then, once the interviewer says they dislike it too, persuade them to do it anyway.
What is the most complex situation, technical or otherwise, that you have handled?
